title: break, continue, return, and labels
hook: Jump statements move execution elsewhere: break exits a loop or switch, continue skips to the next iteration, return exits a function, and labels let you break or continue an outer loop — a feature C# also supports but many developers forget exists.

blocks.text: A **jump statement** transfers control. **break** exits the innermost loop or switch (or a labeled statement). **continue** skips the rest of the current loop iteration. **return** exits the current function and optionally provides a value. **Labels** (`outer:`) name a statement so `break outer` or `continue outer` targets an enclosing loop — useful for nested search loops. JavaScript has no **goto** like C# — labels replace most structured goto needs.

entries.plainDefinition: Exits the innermost switch, loop, or labeled statement immediately.
entries.example: break; inside switch prevents fall-through to the next case.

entries.plainDefinition: Skips remaining statements in the current loop iteration and jumps to the next iteration.
entries.example: continue; after logging a poison message skips processing for that item.

entries.plainDefinition: Ends function execution and optionally passes a value to the caller.
entries.example: return null; early when validation fails — guard clause pattern.

entries.plainDefinition: An identifier prefixing a loop: outer: for (...) { break outer; }
entries.example: Breaks out of nested loops without extra boolean flags.

sections.heading: Why jumps beat deeply nested conditionals

blocks.text: In a batch processor, **continue** after logging a bad record is clearer than nesting three if levels. **return** early when validation fails instead of wrapping the happy path in else. **break** exits a search loop when the target is found. These patterns keep code flat and readable. Labeled break/continue is rare but honest for matrix search — prefer extracting a function when labels hurt readability.

blocks.title: C# comparison
blocks.body: C# break/continue/return behave similarly. C# goto case handles switch fall-through; JavaScript uses break or stacked cases. Both languages allow labeled break/continue on loops. Neither allows jumping into a block from outside.

items.title: Unlabeled break/continue
items.body: Targets the innermost enclosing loop or switch.

items.title: Labeled break/continue
items.body: Targets the statement with the matching label — must be a loop.

items.title: return
items.body: Exits the entire function — not just the loop. Arrow functions use concise return without braces.

items.title: finally interaction
items.body: return inside try still runs finally before the function actually returns.

diagram.title: Jump targets in nested loops
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[outer loop label] --> B[inner loop]
  B --> C{break}
  C -->|unlabeled| D[Exit inner only]
  C -->|break outer| E[Exit both loops]
  B --> F{continue}
  F -->|unlabeled| G[Next inner iteration]
  F -->|continue outer| H[Next outer iteration]

snippet.label: continue and return in batch processing
snippet.explanation: continue skips one iteration. return exits the function immediately — early return guard pattern matches C# style.

snippet.label: break in switch and search loop
snippet.explanation: break exits switch case or loop. Without break in switch, fall-through continues — unlike C# compile-time enforcement.

snippet.label: Labeled break for nested matrix search
snippet.explanation: break outer exits both loops. Alternative: extract findInMatrix() and return early — often cleaner in production.

snippet.label: Arrow function implicit return
snippet.explanation: Concise arrow bodies return an expression without return keyword. finally always runs before the return value is delivered.

blocks.title: Jump statements across languages
rows: goto case in switch; general goto limited

blocks.title: Top pitfalls
blocks.body: Forgetting break in switch cases. Using continue inside forEach callback — it does not skip the outer loop, only ends the callback. Using return inside forEach expecting to exit the outer function — it does not. Overusing labels when a helper function with return is clearer. Assuming break inside finally prevents return — finally still runs.

blocks.title: forEach vs for...of control
blocks.body: break and continue work in for/for...of/while. They do NOT work inside Array.prototype.forEach callbacks — use for...of or a regular for loop when you need to break early.

interviewTakeaways: break exits innermost loop/switch; labeled break exits named outer loop.
continue skips to next iteration; labeled continue jumps outer loop iteration.
return exits the function; arrow functions allow concise expression return.
60s: No goto in JS. break switch cases or fall through. continue/return do not work in forEach — use for...of. finally runs before return delivers.
Follow-up: how does return inside try/finally affect the returned value?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'return inside forEach stops the outer function' — only returns from the callback.
Weak: 'break works everywhere' — not inside forEach; use for...of instead.
Strong: 'Guard with return early. continue for skip-one. break switch always. Labels for nested break — or extract a function.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: C# requires break or goto case. JavaScript switch allows silent fall-through — document intentional cases. Both support labeled break/continue.
TypeScript infers return types on functions with return statements. Early return narrows union types in control flow analysis — similar to C# pattern matching benefits later.
